items.key: ai:why 'challengers' star mike faist disappeared from spotlight for 2 years after breakout role
items.text: Why ‘Challengers’ star Mike Faist disappeared from spotlight for 2 years after breakout role
items.article: Actor Mike Faist explained why he disappeared from the spotlight for two years after his breakout role in 2024's "Challengers." See more of our coverage in your search results. Mike Faist revealed he disappeared from Hollywood for two years after his breakout role in the 2024 film “Challengers” due to the pressures of the spotlight. “It became very apparent to me, there’s a moment of just needing to recalibrate probably for myself,” Faist told GQ Hype in an interview published Wednesday while promoting his new Netflix series, “East of Eden.” The 34-year-old explained that “there’s so much noise in this industry and in the world,” and pointed out that a lot of other actors like to “double down” when they have a hit project and “get onto the next thing.” “They want this momentum,” Faist said, before admitting, “I don’t think that I have that kind of stamina. I’m not necessarily a marathon runner.” Faist stated that he struggled with the “public gaze” when he was promoting the tennis film with co-stars Zendaya and Josh O’Connor.

items.text: Manchester United 'make left-back decision' ahead of January transfer window
items.article: Defender set for new deal as problem position persists Manchester United are set to extend Harry Amass ’ contract ahead of the January transfer window. The Red Devils are short on senior left-back options, particularly after Patrick Dorgu’s injury scare on international duty with Denmark earlier this week. The former Lecce man has been the go-to backup to Luke Shaw when the No23 has been sidelined this term, and Michael Carrick has found himself lacking in depth at full-back. Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui, natural right-backs, have both filled in in that position before, but now it appears that United are set to hand Amass, the academy graduate, fresh terms in a bid to shore up their left flank. The 19-year-old looked set to depart Old Trafford in the summer, with Burnley reportedly interested in a permanent move after the young defender had had loan spells at Sheffield Wednesday and Norwich City. Now, the Manchester Evening News claims that he could be set to extend his stay at his boyhood club, with United set to trigger a 12-month extension clause in his current contract.

I would like to be emailed about offers, event and updates from Evening Standard. Read our privacy notice . In 2007, the first Byron opened. It was a time when burgers were mostly the preserve of McDonald’s, Burger King and the odd country pub; when caramelised onions were a new, exciting topping and nobody had argued about whether brioche buns work with beef (they don’t). Gourmet Burger Kitchen existed, though only as a single restaurant in Battersea. Byron, founded by old Etonian Tom Byng, put forward a “better burger”, one inspired by America and different to the rest. It went well. But Byron’s popularity was part of its downfall. It expanded quickly — there were 70 sites by 2018. Some claimed the quality waned. And soon countless other burger brands opened and the public started to go elsewhere. It’s safe to say Byron lost its way and years of scandal, administration, buyouts and uncertainty followed. Akshat Tibrewala, 22, says the brand can make a stunning comeback. The entrepreneur is reviving the burger chain with renewed gusto. The idea, he says, is to make Byron “exciting again”, with a new menu and new-look restaurants. items.text: The dangers of politicians being 'too online' - or not online enough
items.article: In an era when reputations can be made or broken with a single post, getting the balance right is tricky. The dangers of politicians being 'too online' - or not online enough In early 2015, flower crowns started appearing on Ed Miliband's head. Petals and hearts were photoshopped on to the then-Labour leader by the "Milifandom", a movement of young, mostly female, voters sharing romanticised images on Twitter to protest against Miliband's "distorted media portrayal". It was the brainchild of Abby Tomlinson, a 17-year-old sixth-form student, who came to the defence of the man she called "Milibae". The hashtag #Milifandom trended. Then Labour lost the 2015 election. This prompted David Cameron, whose Conservatives increased their number of seats, to boast: "Britain and Twitter are not the same thing." Tomlinson later told me that having her hopes of Milibae in No10 dashed had made her a "political pessimist", after realising winning over voters online "doesn't happen in a day, a week or even months, it's going to take years". More than a decade on and she is again using social media to big up a Labour leader, but this time in the heart of government. She sits in the press office in No 12 Downing Street as head of content for Andy Burnham. items.key: ai:eon given the green light to buy ovo - what does it mean for customers?
items.text: Eon given the green light to buy Ovo - what does it mean for customers?
items.article: Six energy businesses currently hold more than 90% of the UK's household energy market. This is going down to five. German energy provider Eon has been given the green light to buy UK firm Ovo and create one of the country's largest energy suppliers. The competition regulator today waved through Eon's bid in the latest sign of consolidation in the energy sector as the number of main suppliers falls to five. Eon has about 5.6million customers in the UK. Once it acquires Ovo, the combined group's customer base is expected to be around 9.6million, potentially making it the largest energy provider in the UK. Earlier this year, Eon boss Chris Norbury said greater scale would allow the combined group to improve the range of products and help bring energy bills down. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) today said that the deal would not reduce competition in the market. But when energy bills are forecast to soar, and the number of suppliers is falling, should customers be worried?

items.key: ai:burnham's 'manchesterism' got him to no 10 - but will it work for the uk?
items.text: Burnham's 'Manchesterism' got him to No 10 - but will it work for the UK?
items.article: Economics editor Faisal Islam examines whether the north-west city can be a template for the entire country. Burnham's 'Manchesterism' got him to No 10 - but will it work for the UK? It was just five months ago when Andy Burnham retreated to his mayor's office in Manchester, having been blocked by Labour's ruling executive from standing for parliament. When I met him there a few weeks later, he told me he planned to deal with his disappointment with some ambitious plans for his city region. Burnham told me he wanted to appeal directly to Fifa to host the final of the women's football World Cup in 2035 Manchester instead of Wembley. "Imagine how electrifying that is for any girl growing up in the north of England," he said. He said he was also joining forces with other mayors for a "Great Northern" Olympic bid across the north of England, and a plan was also afoot to host the Ryder Cup in Bolton. Sports bodies needed "re-educating" about the rest of the country, he said. Manchester has already poached the Brit Awards from London after half a century in the capital.

items.key: ai:the real reason your mounjaro has stopped working: dr philippa kaye reveals diet supplement that can boost your jabs, the part of the body you must inject and why it may be time to switch to a different weight loss drug
items.text: The real reason your Mounjaro has stopped working: DR PHILIPPA KAYE reveals diet supplement that can boost your jabs, the part of the body you MUST inject and why it may be time to switch to a different weight loss drug
items.article: Weight-loss injections are some of the most revolutionary medicines in modern times - but they are not perfect. By DR PHILIPPA KAYE, GP, AUTHOR AND CAMPAIGNER Published: 12:09, 28 April 2026 | Updated: 12:04, 8 May 2026 Weight-loss injections are some of the most revolutionary medicines in modern times – but they are not perfect. Millions of Britons and Americans now take Mounjaro and Wegovy, which can help obese patients lose as much as a fifth of their body weight in a year. The data shows that the majority of these patients are women who pay for the appetite-suppressing jabs through private clinics. For any woman above a certain age this will hardly come as a shock – we are all too familiar with the pressure to remain thin, even as the demands of mid-life accumulate. For patients, these drugs can be life-changing, allowing them to lose more weight than they ever thought possible.
